title: 10 Caching Concepts Every Backend Engineer Must Know
summary: A ten-concept listicle on backend caching: read and write strategies, expiry and eviction, invalidation and stampedes, CDN and distributed caches, and consistency. Each concept gets a worked example, trade-offs and an interview takeaway.

chapters.title: 10 Caching Concepts Every Backend Engineer Must Know
points: Cover promise: 10 concepts, ordered from foundational to advanced
Lineup part 1: Cache-Aside, Write-Through, Write-Back, TTL and Expiry, Eviction Policies
Lineup part 2: Cache Invalidation, Cache Stampede, CDN Caching, Distributed Caches, Cache Consistency
Why caching matters: a Redis read takes ~0.5 ms, a typical database query 5-50 ms, so a 95% hit rate cuts average latency about 10x

chapters.title: Cache-Aside
points: What it is: the app checks the cache first, loads from the database on a miss, then fills the cache itself (lazy loading)
Why it exists: the database is slow and overloaded by repeated reads of the same hot rows; the cache stays a disposable side store
Used for: read-heavy data such as user profiles, product pages, config and lookup tables
How it works, worked example: GET user:42 misses in Redis, then SELECT * FROM users WHERE id=42 (12 ms), then SET user:42 <json> EX 300; the next read returns in 0.4 ms
Benefits: only requested data is cached; a cache crash only slows requests, it never loses data; simple to add to existing code
Things to consider: the first request after a miss is slow (cold start); data can go stale between writes; every call site needs the check-and-fill logic
Interview takeaway: the default read pattern, where the app owns cache logic and writes update the DB then delete the key, not set it

chapters.title: Write-Through
points: What it is: every write goes to the cache and the database together, synchronously, before the write is acknowledged
Why it exists: cache-aside leaves a stale window after writes; write-through keeps the cache current at write time
Used for: data read right after it is written, such as account balances, session state and inventory counts
How it works, worked example: UPDATE stock SET qty=7 WHERE sku='A1' and SET stock:A1 7 happen in one write path; the client gets OK only when both succeed, so the next read hits fresh data
Benefits: reads are always fresh and fast; no stale window; the cache is always warm for written keys
Things to consider: write latency is the sum of both writes; data nobody reads still fills the cache; a failure between the two writes needs retry or rollback
Interview takeaway: trades slower writes for read consistency; often paired with cache-aside for reads, and it is not the same as write-back

chapters.title: Write-Back
points: What it is: writes land in the cache only and are flushed to the database later in batches (also called write-behind)
Why it exists: the database write is the bottleneck; absorbing bursts in memory gives much higher write throughput
Used for: high-volume counters, view counts, metrics, game scores and activity logs
How it works, worked example: 10,000 INCR views:post9 calls in 1 s sit in Redis; a worker flushes one UPDATE posts SET views=views+10000 every 5 s, so 10,000 writes become 1
Benefits: very low write latency; coalesces repeated writes to the same key; shields the database from spikes
Things to consider: unflushed data is lost if the cache node dies; the database lags behind the cache; needs a durable queue or AOF persistence and a flush retry policy
Interview takeaway: fastest writes but weakest durability, so use it only for data you can afford to lose a few seconds of

chapters.title: TTL and Expiry
points: What it is: a time-to-live is a per-key lifetime after which the cache treats the entry as gone
Why it exists: it bounds how stale data can get and stops the cache growing forever, even if invalidation fails
Used for: sessions (30 min), OTP codes (5 min), API rate-limit windows (60 s), product prices (5 min)
How it works, worked example: SET otp:9876 481516 EX 300 then TTL otp:9876 returns 297; after 300 s GET returns nil. Redis combines lazy expiry on access with a background sampler of random keys
Benefits: automatic cleanup; a hard staleness bound; a cheap safety net behind explicit invalidation
Things to consider: a TTL too short means low hit rate; too long means stale reads; identical TTLs expire together, so add jitter (e.g. 300 s plus random 0-60 s)
Interview takeaway: TTL is the staleness budget; pick it from how wrong the data may be, and always add jitter

chapters.title: Eviction Policies (LRU, LFU)
points: What it is: the rule that picks which key to drop when the cache hits its memory limit; LRU drops the least recently used, LFU the least frequently used
Why it exists: memory is finite, so a full cache must discard entries to admit new ones
Used for: bounded caches such as Redis with maxmemory set, in-process caches and CPU or page caches

How it works, worked example: capacity 3, access A B C A then add D. LRU evicts B (oldest touch). LFU counts A=2, B=1, C=1 and evicts B or C, never A. Redis: maxmemory-policy allkeys-lru or allkeys-lfu
Benefits: LRU is O(1) with a hash map plus doubly linked list and suits recency-biased traffic; LFU protects long-term hot keys from one-off scans

Things to consider: LRU is polluted by a single big scan; LFU keeps formerly hot keys forever without counter decay; Redis uses approximate sampling, not exact order; noeviction returns errors when full
Interview takeaway: be able to code an O(1) LRU, and say LFU wins on stable hot sets while LRU wins on shifting ones

chapters.title: Cache Invalidation
points: What it is: removing or updating cached entries when the source data changes, so readers do not see stale values
Why it exists: a cache is a copy, and copies drift; the proverbial hardest problem is knowing when a copy is wrong
Used for: product edits, profile updates, permission changes and price changes
How it works, worked example: on UPDATE products SET price=19 WHERE id=7 the service runs DEL product:7, and also DEL category:shoes:page1 because that list embeds the price
Benefits: bounded staleness when done on write; targeted deletes keep the rest of the cache warm; versioned keys such as product:7:v12 avoid deletes entirely
Things to consider: derived and list keys are easy to forget; delete then update races can re-cache an old value; events can be lost, so keep a TTL fallback
Interview takeaway: prefer delete over update on write, track dependent keys, and keep a TTL as the backstop

chapters.title: Cache Stampede
points: What it is: when a hot key expires, many concurrent requests all miss and hit the database together (thundering herd)
Why it exists: expiry is synchronized and the miss path is unprotected, so every waiting request recomputes the same value
Used for: protecting hot keys such as the homepage feed, trending lists and expensive aggregates

How it works, worked example: key home:feed expires at 12:00:00 with 2,000 req/s; all 2,000 run a 300 ms query at once and the DB spikes. Fix: SET lock:home NX EX 10; the winner rebuilds, the rest wait 50 ms and re-read
Benefits: request coalescing or locking turns N queries into 1; TTL jitter spreads expiries; stale-while-revalidate serves the old value during refresh
Things to consider: locks need a timeout or a crashed rebuilder blocks everyone; waiters need a retry cap; probabilistic early refresh needs tuning
Interview takeaway: name three fixes: lock or single-flight, TTL jitter and early or background refresh

chapters.title: CDN Caching
points: What it is: caching content on edge servers near users, controlled by HTTP headers, so requests never reach your origin
Why it exists: distance costs latency (about 150 ms across oceans) and origin bandwidth is expensive
Used for: static assets, images, video segments, public API responses and cacheable HTML

How it works, worked example: response header Cache-Control: public, max-age=31536000, immutable on app.4f9a1c.js (hashed filename); an HTML page gets s-maxage=60, stale-while-revalidate=300. First hit is X-Cache: MISS, later hits are HIT from the edge
Benefits: lower latency worldwide; large origin offload (often 90%+ hit ratio); absorbs traffic spikes and DDoS
Things to consider: purging is slow or costs money, so use content-hashed filenames; keep cookies out of cacheable responses; Vary headers can fragment the cache
Interview takeaway: control CDN behavior with Cache-Control, using immutable hashed assets and short s-maxage for dynamic pages

chapters.title: Distributed Caches (Redis, Memcached)
points: What it is: a cache shared by many app servers over the network, spread across several nodes
Why it exists: per-process caches duplicate data, diverge between instances, and are lost on each deploy
Used for: shared sessions, rate limiting, leaderboards, pub/sub and shared hot data

How it works, worked example: Redis Cluster splits keys into 16,384 hash slots; slot = CRC16(key) mod 16384, so user:42 maps to one node and each node has a replica. Memcached clients use consistent hashing across nodes
Benefits: horizontal scaling of memory and throughput; one shared view of the data; Redis adds replication, persistence and rich types (hash, sorted set, stream)

Things to consider: Memcached is multi-threaded and simple but offers only strings and no persistence; Redis is mostly single-threaded per shard; a network hop costs ~0.5 ms; hot keys overload one node
Interview takeaway: pick Redis for data structures and persistence, Memcached for plain, simple, high-throughput key-value caching, and know how keys map to nodes

chapters.title: Cache Consistency
points: What it is: how closely cached copies match the database and each other, from eventual up to strong consistency
Why it exists: updating a cache and a database are two separate operations, and failures or races can leave them disagreeing
Used for: deciding what staleness each feature tolerates: feeds can lag seconds, balances and stock cannot

How it works, worked example: race: T1 reads old price 10 from the DB, T2 writes 12 and deletes the key, T1 then SETs 10 into the cache and the stale value lives until TTL. Fixes: short TTL, delayed double delete (delete again after 500 ms), or CDC streaming DB changes to invalidate
Benefits: choosing the level per data type gives speed where staleness is fine; versioned values detect stale writes; CDC makes invalidation reliable
Things to consider: strong consistency means skipping the cache or using locks, which costs latency; replica lag adds a second stale source; cross-region caches are only eventually consistent
Interview takeaway: caching trades consistency for speed, so state your tolerated staleness per data type and a mitigation (TTL, CDC or versioning)

chapters.title: Caching Cheatsheet
points: Read patterns: cache-aside is the default (app loads on miss); write-through gives fresh reads; write-back gives the fastest writes with a loss risk
Expiry: set a TTL on everything, add jitter, and size it from the tolerated staleness
Eviction: LRU for recency, LFU for stable hot sets; Redis uses maxmemory plus allkeys-lru or allkeys-lfu
Invalidation: delete on write, remember list and derived keys, and keep a TTL backstop
Stampede fixes: lock or single-flight, jittered TTL, stale-while-revalidate, early refresh
CDN: Cache-Control public, max-age, s-maxage and immutable; hashed filenames avoid purges
Redis vs Memcached: Redis has types, persistence and replication; Memcached is simple, multi-threaded and string-only
Consistency: pick the level per feature; use delayed double delete, versioning or CDC against stale races
